title: 六级讲话讲座：比例、叙述者与检索
instruction: 听完整一节三篇讲话/讲座及各段后读出的问题，依次选择最佳答案。音频中材料和问题各读一遍，卷面只印四个选项。本原创使用节内编号1—10，各段对应1—3、4—6、7—10题。播放器可回听，正式单次听辨条件未强制。
audio_introduction: Section C. You will hear three recordings of lectures or talks. After each, you will hear questions. Each recording and each question will be spoken only once. Choose the best answer from A, B, C and D.
source_form_notice: 六级形式参照2024年12月第一套转载Section C：3段、3/3/4共10回应、每题四选；原创采用节内编号，问题只在录音与作者区。全部自有虚构内容及本机合成试听，非原考试原声；未独立教研/听辨/学生难度或产品等值验证。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: Consider an imaginary cooperative that wishes to report participation in its annual meeting. Its first report says that attendance rose from forty people to sixty. That sounds like an improvement, and as a statement about the number in the room it is perfectly clear. But the cooperative also gained new members during the year. It had eighty members at the first meeting and two hundred at the second. The attendance rate therefore fell from fifty per cent to thirty per cent. There is no contradiction between the larger crowd and the lower rate. They answer different questions. The count tells us how many attended. The rate relates that count to a defined membership. Which is more useful depends on what we are trying to understand. If we need to know how many chairs to provide, the count is directly relevant. If we are discussing how widely members were represented, the rate may add information that the count hides. Even then, we should ask who was included in the membership list and whether that definition stayed the same. A percentage does not remove those decisions. Now suppose someone suggests making the report look better by describing the extra twenty attendees but omitting the expanding membership. The problem is not that the count becomes mathematically false. It is that a true statement is being invited to carry an unsupported implication about broader participation. A responsible report can print both measures and say what each describes. It can also discuss why some members did not attend without pretending that their reasons can be read from the percentage alone. The point of this example is to resist the search for one number that settles every argument. Before choosing a measure, state the question. Then make the population and comparison visible enough for another person to see whether the number actually answers it.

questions.spoken_question: What happened to the cooperative’s attendance rate?
options: A
It rose from thirty to fifty per cent.
B
It remained at fifty per cent.
C
It fell from fifty to thirty per cent.
D
It fell because fewer people attended.

questions.spoken_question: When is the attendance count especially useful in the example?
options: A
When deciding how many chairs are needed.
B
When proving why absent members stayed away.
C
When replacing the membership definition entirely.
D
When claiming every member was equally represented.
questions.rationale: A椅数依人数；B比例不能读原因，C仍需人口定义，Dcount不证公平代表。

questions.spoken_question: What is the speaker’s main recommendation?
options: A
Always publish the measure that looks most encouraging.
B
Avoid all percentages when reporting a meeting.
C
Use membership growth as proof of attendance quality.
D
Choose measures for stated questions and show their population.
questions.rationale: D先问题/界群体比较；A明反，B不禁百分，C非质量证明。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: In a fictional literature seminar, the class reads a story told through a traveller's notebook. On the first page, the traveller describes a host as unfriendly because he speaks very little. Later, we learn that the host had been trying to protect the traveller from overhearing news she was not ready to receive. Several students say that the first page is simply wrong and should be ignored. The seminar leader asks them to distinguish an observation from the interpretation attached to it. The host did speak little. The traveller's explanation for the silence was uncertain. A narrative can preserve the observation while inviting us to reconsider what it meant. This distinction also changes how we think about the narrator. A mistaken interpretation does not necessarily make every event in the notebook false. Nor does it automatically tell us that the author shares the traveller's first judgement. The author has arranged later information that allows a reader to see beyond it. The class then examines a second moment. The traveller claims to have understood the host immediately, but her earlier entries show repeated confusion. Here the interest lies in the distance between the narrator's later account of herself and the record the story has already given us. We are not required to diagnose the character or accuse a real person of dishonesty. We are being asked to notice how different parts of the narrative qualify one another. One student proposes rewriting the opening so that the traveller understands everything from the start. That would remove the inconsistency, but it would also remove the reader's experience of discovering the limits of the traveller's view. The seminar leader suggests that an apparent weakness in a narrator can be part of the design of a strong narrative. Reading carefully means asking which voice makes a claim, what that voice could know at the time, and how the rest of the story asks us to treat the claim.

questions.spoken_question: What distinction does the seminar leader make about the host’s silence?
options: A
The host’s silence never occurred in the story.
B
The observed silence is separate from the traveller’s explanation of it.
C
The traveller had access to all the host’s intentions.
D
An unfriendly host must always speak very little.
questions.rationale: B观察少语与unfriendly解释分开；A确少语，C后来才知，D不是少语必不友好。

questions.spoken_question: Why need the author not share the narrator’s first judgement?
options: A
The author has removed all later information.
B
The narrator is not allowed to express opinions.
C
Later information is arranged so readers can look beyond that judgement.
D
Every notebook story is a factual autobiography.
questions.rationale: C后据使读者超前见原限；A反，B可主观，D明确虚构非自传通则。

questions.spoken_question: What would be lost if the opening gave the traveller complete understanding?
options: A
The reader’s gradual discovery of the limits of her viewpoint.
B
The host’s ability to appear anywhere in the story.
C
All distinction between spoken and written language.
D
The possibility of printing the notebook in chronological order.
questions.rationale: A去除读者发现视角局限经历；B/C/D非改写必然。

turns.speaker: R
turns.text: Imagine you are designing a search tool for a collection of local photographs. A visitor types the name of a bridge. The collection contains a photograph filed under an older name for the same bridge, so an exact match returns nothing. The first improvement seems obvious: accept both names. That is useful, but it introduces a question about how the result should be presented. If the tool silently replaces every old name with the new one, a researcher may lose information about how a photograph was originally described. The design team therefore keeps the catalogue wording visible and adds the alternative as a searchable link. Searching can become more forgiving without rewriting the historical record. Now consider a query for market. Some photographs show a market square, while others show a shop with market in its name. A high position in the results cannot by itself decide which sense the visitor intended. The interface can offer filters or a short explanation of why a result matched. It should not pretend that the first result is necessarily the answer. Finally, suppose the team judges success only by whether visitors click something. A click may mean that a promising item was found. It may also mean that the brief result description was too vague to reject. The team asks visitors to complete a small locating task and explain whether the item they opened met the stated need. This adds work to the evaluation, but it relates the observed action to the purpose of the search. None of these choices promises a perfect catalogue or an infallible interpretation of every query. The design separates three responsibilities: preserving what the collection says, helping a visitor express a request, and providing enough context to judge a returned item. When those responsibilities are confused, a tool can appear efficient while making the collection harder to understand. When they are distinguished, the team has a clearer way to discuss which problem a particular change is intended to solve.

questions.spoken_question: Why does the team retain old wording in the catalogue display?
options: A
To prevent anyone from searching by the new name.
B
To preserve how the photograph was originally described.
C
To prove that modern place names are always inaccurate.
D
To remove the need for links between names.
questions.rationale: B保原描述但加别名索引；A新旧均搜，C非现代都错，D恰加链接。

questions.spoken_question: What does the market example illustrate?
options: A
Every searcher wants the oldest possible photograph.
B
Exact spelling is the only obstacle to useful search.
C
Different possible meanings of a query may need clarification.
D
Shop photographs should never appear in a collection.
questions.rationale: Cmarket广场或店名不同义；A/D无，B超出拼写。

questions.spoken_question: Why is a click alone an uncertain sign of search success?
options: A
All visitors click only after finding an exact answer.
B
A click proves that the catalogue description is complete.
C
The collection cannot record which items were opened.
D
It can reflect either a useful match or insufficient result information.
questions.rationale: D可能合需也可能摘要太糊不能排，A/B把点击误当充分，C可观察click。

questions.spoken_question: What is the speaker’s central argument?
options: A
Search design should distinguish preservation, requesting and judging results.
B
A search tool should replace every historical description automatically.
C
The first returned item must be treated as a correct answer.
D
Evaluation should ignore the purpose behind a visitor’s action.
questions.rationale: A三责任分开主旨；B/C/D分别明确反。
